summary:
We built an interactive web tool that screens all of Earth for analogs of two destinations: the Artemis III Moon base and Mars exploration zones. No single place can rehearse a whole mission, so we scored all 19,002 one- degree land cells.
 The tool works in two stages. A global thermal screen ranks every land cell on mean cold, cold extremes and thermal swing using NASA POWER climatology, producing an Analog Similarity Index from 0 to 100 with weight sliders. Clicking any point on the globe then requests that coordinate from the NASA POWER API live, adding pressure, rainfall, humidity, ultraviolet index and wind, each compared to the moon or Mars reference value.
 The screen surfaced five new candidates, including Karakul in the Pamir and the Lut Desert kaluts, alongside six established analogs. Eleven dossiers explain what works what breaks and what to test every number and image traced to NASA.
 This matters because a global search that would take months runs in seconds, and because the tool is honest: it states openly where the analogy fails, including that Earth's thinnest air is still about 94 times the pressure on Mars.
details:
Our team developed an interactive web prototype for exploring Earth environments that may support preparation for future Moon and Mars missions. We provided the project goals, design ideas, requirements, and selected source materials, and used SI-assisted development to help turn these inputs into a working application.

The project focuses on lunar south-polar environments and Mars exploration targets. Rather than presenting one Earth location as a perfect planetary twin, it compares different kinds of similarity and recommends considering a combination of sites for different research and testing needs.

How it works?

The prototype combines a global thermal screen with an on-demand point scanner . Its preprocessed global layer covers 19,002 one-degree land cells and uses NASA POWER temperature data to compare cold conditions and temperature variation through a project-specific Analog Similarity Index from 0 to 100.

Users can switch between Moon and Mars modes and adjust the importance of the available comparison criteria. The global layer is a thermal screening tool, not a comprehensive global assessment of geology, atmospheric conditions, or mission suitability.

Clicking a location on the globe requests point-specific environmental data directly from the NASA POWER API. The scanner adds information such as surface pressure, precipitation, humidity, and wind, while explaining where an Earth environment cannot reproduce the target conditions.

Eleven site dossiers provide context beyond the global thermal ranking. Five candidate locations featured in the project are Kara-Kul in the Pamir, the Dalangtan playa in the Qaidam Basin, the Lut Desert kaluts, the Saririaky anorthosite massif, and Lonar Crater; six comparison locations are Haughton, Atacama, Death Valley, the McMurdo Dry Valleys, Mauna Kea, and Lanzarote.

The dossiers describe useful similarities, important differences, and potential applications for field research or equipment testing. These are candidates for further investigation, not a claim that the project has independently proven previously unknown analog sites.

A comparison slider places real Earth imagery alongside lunar or Martian imagery. It helps users explore visual similarities while keeping appearance separate from scientific suitability.

Intended impact and benefits

The intended users include researchers, students, and teams planning preliminary analog field studies. The prototype helps them explore a broad set of locations, compare priorities, and identify questions that require more detailed investigation.

Faster exploration: Preprocessed layers make initial comparisons accessible through a browser.

Transparency: Source information and explanations help users understand what the scores represent and what they leave out.

Broader discovery: Users can investigate locations beyond the familiar examples included in the dossiers.

Complementary site selection: Different locations can support different testing objectives instead of being treated as interchangeable planetary replicas.

The application is built with HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript, with SI-assisted implementation guided by the team’s requirements and design direction. The interactive globe uses d3.js and topojson-client, with Natural Earth geographic data distributed through world-atlas.

Python scripts were used to retrieve and process NASA POWER climate data. The application runs in the visitor’s browser without a dedicated backend, and FFmpeg was used for the demonstration screen recording.

Photographic material comes from NASA resources and is credited in the project. No SI-generated photographs were used.

The project brings Moon and Mars comparisons into one interface rather than treating them as separate experiences. Adjustable priorities, on-demand data requests, site dossiers, and side-by-side imagery connect numerical comparisons with explanations that a non-specialist can explore.

Its central idea is to make the limits of an analogy visible alongside its strengths. A useful result is not simply the highest score, but a clearer understanding of which location could support which experiment.

We considered differences between thermal, geological, atmospheric, and operational similarity, as well as the need for mission-specific priorities. We also considered accessibility, safety, logistics, data resolution, API availability, and the risk of presenting a simplified score as more conclusive than it is.

The current application is a first-pass exploratory prototype. It does not replace specialist assessment, field measurements, controlled-environment testing, or a full mission-site selection process.

Using of Super Intelligence (SI)

Our team set the project goals and provided design ideas, requirements, prompts, and selected data and reference materials. We used Perplexity Computer as a development assistant to help turn these inputs into a working prototype, explore implementation options, and refine the presentation.

SI assistance included generating and debugging HTML, CSS, and JavaScript; helping prepare Python scripts for retrieving and processing NASA POWER data; suggesting technical improvements; and drafting or refining explanatory text and demo materials. The team guided this process through instructions, feedback, and revisions. SI contributed to implementation and refinement, while the team directed the project and remains responsible for the submitted work.

The scientific information and imagery used in the project come from the cited NASA resources, not from SI-generated observations or photographs. Source references and explicit limitations help users distinguish the underlying evidence from the prototype’s interpretations and similarity scores.

No SI-generated photographs were used. The demonstration video is a recording of the application made with FFmpeg, rather than SI- generated footage. SI was not used to generate or modify NASA logos, flags, or mission identifiers.
